stem: A 4-year-old boy has had two weeks of intermittent bright red blood on the stool without pain. He is otherwise well and slightly pale, with no pigmented spots on his lips or mouth. Colonoscopy shows a single smooth, pedunculated polyp in the rectum, which is removed.
oneliner: 4M + 2 wk painless bright red rectal bleeding + mild pallor + no lip pigmentation + single smooth pedunculated rectal polyp → which histology?
ask: Which histologic finding is most likely in the polyp?

options.A: Crowded tubular glands with dysplastic nuclei
options.C: Arborizing smooth muscle bands in the stalk
options.D: Dilated mucus-filled cysts in inflamed stroma

whyNot.A: A **tubular adenoma** is a dysplastic, premalignant polyp of adults, not a solitary polyp in a **4-year-old**
whyNot.B: **Serrated polyps** arise in adults, not as a single rectal polyp in a **4-year-old**
whyNot.C: That is a **Peutz-Jeghers** polyp; he has **no lip or mouth pigmentation** and a **single rectal** polyp
whyNot.E: That is a **carcinoid**, a submucosal tumor of adults, not a **pedunculated rectal polyp** in a young child

answer: Juvenile (hamartomatous) polyp: cystic mucus-filled glands in inflamed lamina propria, no dysplasia
why: A **solitary rectal polyp** with **painless bleeding** in a child under 10 is a **juvenile polyp**, a hamartoma. It has **cystically dilated, mucus-filled glands** in an **inflamed, edematous lamina propria** and **no dysplasia**, so it is almost never premalignant.

idea.rule: Juvenile polyp = child + painless rectal bleeding + cystic glands in inflamed stroma, no dysplasia.
also: The commonest colorectal polyp in children, usually rectal
May twist and autoamputate, passing in the stool
Multiple juvenile polyps (juvenile polyposis, SMAD4 or BMPR1A) raise colorectal cancer risk

stem: A 23-year-old woman has had 6 years of intermittent fever, crampy right lower abdominal pain and loose stools, and she has a perianal fistula. After a severe flare, a segment of ileum is resected. At surgery several diseased loops are stuck together.
oneliner: 23F + 6 y fever, crampy RLQ pain, loose stools + perianal fistula + resected ileum, loops stuck together → which gross finding?
ask: Which gross finding is most likely in the resected bowel?

options.A: Continuous inflammation from the rectum upward with pseudopolyps
options.C: Thick, narrowed skip segments wrapped in creeping fat
options.D: Yellow-white pseudomembranes of fibrin and neutrophils on intact mucosa
options.E: Mucosal outpouchings pushing through the muscularis of the sigmoid colon

whyNot.A: **Ulcerative colitis**: continuous mucosal disease of the colon from the rectum; her disease is in the **ileum** with a **perianal fistula**
whyNot.B: **Amebic colitis**: flask-shaped ulcers after a diarrheal exposure; she has **6 years of relapsing disease with a fistula**
whyNot.D: **C. difficile colitis**: pseudomembranes after antibiotics, acute, not a **years-long course with fistula**
whyNot.E: **Diverticulosis**: sigmoid pouches in older adults, not **fistulizing ileal disease** at 23

answer: Skip areas of thickened, narrowed bowel with creeping fat (Crohn disease)
why: Relapsing fever, pain and loose stools with a **perianal fistula** and an inflamed ileum fit **Crohn disease**. Transmural inflammation makes the wall **thick and narrow** and makes loops **stick together**; diseased segments alternate with normal bowel (**skip lesions**), and fat creeps over the serosa.

idea.rule: Crohn disease looks patchy and thick-walled; ulcerative colitis looks continuous and mucosal.
also: Cobblestone mucosa from linear ulcers crossing edematous mucosa
Creeping fat wraps the bowel surface
Strictures and fistulas follow from full-thickness inflammation
Ulcerative colitis stays in the mucosa and submucosa, with pseudopolyps

stem: A 4-year-old girl has blood-streaked stools. She has dark macules on her lips and the inside of her cheeks, and so does her father. Endoscopy shows several polyps in the small bowel and colon, and one is removed.
oneliner: 4F + blood-streaked stools + dark lip and buccal macules, same in father + several small bowel and colon polyps → which histologic finding?
ask: Which histologic finding is most likely in the removed polyp?

options.A: Normal-looking glands over branching bands of smooth muscle
options.B: Dilated, mucus-filled cysts in inflamed stroma
options.C: Crowded tubular glands with hyperchromatic, pencil-shaped nuclei
options.E: Islands of regenerating mucosa between ulcers

whyNot.B: **Juvenile polyp** (cystic glands in inflamed stroma) occurs without **pigmented lip macules** or a family pattern
whyNot.C: **Tubular adenoma** shows **dysplastic nuclei**; a child with **lip and buccal macules shared with her father** has syndromic hamartomas
whyNot.D: **Hyperplastic or serrated polyp** is a mucosal change with **no smooth muscle core**
whyNot.E: **Inflammatory pseudopolyps** need long-standing **ulcerating colitis**, not macules and polyps in a young child

answer: Hamartomatous polyp: normal glands over arborizing smooth muscle
why: Macules on the **lips and buccal mucosa**, polyps through the bowel and an affected parent describe **Peutz-Jeghers syndrome**. Its polyps are **hamartomas**: normal mucosa is thrown over **branching (arborizing) bands of smooth muscle**.

idea.rule: A hamartoma is normal tissue in a disorganized arrangement, so Peutz-Jeghers polyps show normal epithelium on a branching muscle frame.
also: Juvenile polyps are hamartomas too: normal-type glands, cystic and disorganized
Cowden syndrome (PTEN) gives multiple hamartomatous polyps
Pulmonary hamartoma mixes mature cartilage, fat and respiratory epithelium
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is autosomal dominant, from STK11 mutations

stem: A 62-year-old man has a barium study for rectal bleeding. The upper small-bowel loops in the left upper abdomen show a feathery mucosal pattern, while loops further along look smoother.
oneliner: 62M + barium study for rectal bleeding + feathery upper small-bowel loops, smoother distal loops → which feature explains the feathery pattern?
ask: Which structural feature explains the feathery pattern of the upper loops?

options.A: Absence of a circular muscle layer
options.C: Tall circular folds carrying long villi
options.D: Peristalsis that is faster than in the distal loops
options.E: Thin circular and longitudinal muscle layers

whyNot.A: Both muscle layers are present along the whole small bowel; the contrast outlines the **mucosa**, not the muscle
whyNot.B: Fewer villi would give a **smoother** pattern, which is what he has in the **distal** loops
whyNot.D: Motility does not shape the **mucosal pattern** that the contrast coats
whyNot.E: Muscle thickness would not change what **coats the mucosa**; the folds do

answer: Tall plicae circulares with long villi (jejunum)
why: The contrast coats the **mucosa**. The **jejunum** has **tall, numerous plicae circulares** and **long villi**, which give the feathery pattern and the greatest absorptive surface. The ileum has fewer folds and shorter villi, so it looks smoother.

idea.rule: Jejunum: tall folds and long villi for absorption. Ileum: fewer folds, Peyer patches.
also: Peyer patches sit in the ileum
The ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and bile acids
Duodenal Brunner glands are submucosal and secrete alkaline mucus
The ileum has more goblet cells than the jejunum

stem: A 45-year-old man has epigastric pain that comes 1 to 3 hours after meals and wakes him at night, and his stool tests positive for occult blood. Endoscopy shows a 3-cm ulcer in the antrum. Mucosa beside the ulcer shows chronic inflammation, and a rapid urease test on the biopsy is positive. A silver stain of this tissue is examined at high power.
oneliner: 45M + antral ulcer + pain 1-3 h after meals + chronic gastritis beside it + urease-positive biopsy + silver stain → which finding?
ask: Which finding is expected on the silver-stained section?

options.A: Gram-positive cocci in clusters invading the lamina propria
options.B: Budding yeast with pseudohyphae on the mucosal surface
options.C: Foamy macrophages with PAS-positive granules in the lamina propria
options.D: Acid-fast oocysts along the brush border
options.E: Curved, comma-shaped bacilli in the mucus over the surface epithelium

whyNot.A: Tissue invasion by **staphylococci** with abscess formation, not **chronic antral gastritis** with a positive urease test
whyNot.B: **Candida** affects the esophagus and mouth of immunocompromised patients and is not the cause of a **urease-positive** antral ulcer
whyNot.C: **Whipple disease** of the small bowel, where macrophages fill the lamina propria; this biopsy is **gastric**
whyNot.D: **Cryptosporidium** in the small bowel of immunocompromised patients with watery diarrhea, not an antral ulcer

answer: Curved, comma-shaped bacilli in the surface mucus (Helicobacter pylori)
why: An antral ulcer with chronic gastritis beside it and a **positive urease test** points to ***Helicobacter pylori***. It is a curved rod that lives **in the mucus above the surface epithelium**, and silver stains such as **Warthin-Starry or Steiner** make it easy to see.

idea.rule: H. pylori is a curved, urease-producing rod in gastric surface mucus, shown by silver stain.
also: Urease makes ammonia, which buffers acid and drives the urea breath test
It causes chronic antral gastritis and most duodenal ulcers
It raises the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma
Giemsa and immunohistochemical stains also highlight the organism
